newsitem.title: USA: U.S. analyst urges grain export subsidy freeze.
newsitem.headline: U.S. analyst urges grain export subsidy freeze.

text.p: A leading U.S. agricultural trade expert has urged the U.S., European Union and other grain exporting nations to speed up their timetable for reducing grain export subsidies.

In a prepared statement, World Perspectives Inc Chairman Carole Brookins called for the action to commerate the 50th annivesary this year of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, which preceeded the World Trade Organization.

The Uruguay Round trade agreement, which countries began implementing in 1995, requires the U.S. and the E.U. to cut agricultural export subsidy spending by 36 percent over six years. Subsidized tonnage is also required to decline by 21 percent under the pact.

However, any subsidies not used in the early years of the agreement are available for later years, as long as export subsidy spending and tonnages decline to the agreed upon levels in 2000, the sixth year of the pact.
That creates the possibility that there could be an explosion of export subsidy activity just as countries begin a new round of agriculture trade negotiations in 1999.
To prevent that from happening, the U.S., E.U. and others should cap grain export subsidy spending and volume at the year 2000 level beginning in 1998, Brookins said.
This could "easily" be accomplished because world grain demand in recent years has been much stronger than anticipated when the Uruguay Round pact was negotiated, she said.
The U.S. has had not had to subsidized wheat exports for nearly two years and the E.U. has twice imposed taxes on wheat exports over the same period, Brookins said.

Grain export subsidies are likely to be discussed next week at the International Grain Council's meeting in London, which each year draws top-level government and trade representatives from the major grain importing and exporting nations.
U.S. Agriculture Department Secretary Dan Glickman is scheduled to address the meeting.
Meanwhile, current allocations for countries to buy U.S.-subsidized wheat and other farm goods under the Export Enhancement Program expire at the end of the month.
Even though the U.S. has not used EEP for nearly 2 years, the agriculture department is still expected to announce allocations for 1997-98 (July-June) in the coming weeks.

However, prospects for the U.S. to actually resume export subsidies remain dim in the near-term, given a tight domestic supply situation and the high probability that E.U. export subsidies will remain restrained, one analyst said.
